title: Banking app — synchronized for concurrent account access (method vs block, real scenarios)
shortTitle: How do you use synchronized for bank account access?

s1_definition.profdef: In a banking application where multiple users (threads) access the SAME account concurrently, you must synchronize ALL operations that read-and-modify the balance to prevent race conditions. Two approaches: **Synchronized method** — `synchronized void debit()` locks on the Account object for the entire method. Simple but coarse — blocks ALL account operations during ANY operation. **Synchronized block** — `synchronized(account) { balance -= amount; }` locks only the critical section. Better: validation, logging, notification run WITHOUT holding the lock. For real banking: use **per-account locks** (not a global lock) so operations on different accounts run in parallel. For transfers between TWO accounts: acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (by account ID) to prevent deadlock.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh and Priya both try to withdraw from Rajesh's account simultaneously using ATM and mobile. Without synchronization: both read balance Rs.100,000, both withdraw Rs.60,000, both succeed — balance shows Rs.40,000 instead of rejecting one. With synchronization: ATM transaction LOCKS Rajesh's account → checks balance → debits → UNLOCKS. Mobile transaction waits for the lock → checks updated balance → Rs.40,000 < Rs.60,000 → REJECTED. For transfers: lock Rajesh's account FIRST, then Priya's — always in the same order to prevent both sides waiting for each other (deadlock).
s1_definition.oneliner: Per-account lock (not global). Sync block > sync method (shorter lock time). Multi-account transfer: lock in consistent order (by ID) to prevent deadlock.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a banking application where multiple users (threads) access the SAME account concurrently, you must synchronize ALL operations that read-and-modify the balance to prevent race conditions. Two approaches: **Synchronized method** — `synchronized void debit()` locks on the Account object for the entire method. Simple but coarse — blocks ALL account operations during ANY operation. **Synchronized block** — `synchronized(account) { balance -= amount; }` locks only the critical section. Better: validation, logging, notification run WITHOUT holding the lock. For real banking: use **per-account locks** (not a global lock) so operations on different accounts run in parallel. For transfers between TWO accounts: acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (by account ID) to prevent deadlock.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh and Priya both try to withdraw from Rajesh's account simultaneously using ATM and mobile. Without synchronization: both read balance Rs.100,000, both withdraw Rs.60,000, both succeed — balance shows Rs.40,000 instead of rejecting one. With synchronization: ATM transaction LOCKS Rajesh's account → checks balance → debits → UNLOCKS. Mobile transaction waits for the lock → checks updated balance → Rs.40,000 < Rs.60,000 → REJECTED. For transfers: lock Rajesh's account FIRST, then Priya's — always in the same order to prevent both sides waiting for each other (deadlock).

**One line to remember:** Per-account lock (not global). Sync block > sync method (shorter lock time). Multi-account transfer: lock in consistent order (by ID) to prevent deadlock.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The banking API used a single global `synchronized` block for ALL account operations.** 50K users accessing 10K different accounts → all operations serialized through ONE lock → throughput: 200 ops/sec. Fix: per-account lock — each account has its own lock object. Operations on DIFFERENT accounts run in PARALLEL. Throughput: 50K ops/sec. Transfer between two accounts: lock both in consistent order (by account ID) to prevent deadlock when two simultaneous transfers go in opposite directions.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** 100 threads simultaneously debit Rs.1000 from Rajesh (Rs.100,000). Each thread acquires `rajesh.lock`, checks balance, subtracts, releases lock. Serialized per-account. Final: exactly Rs.0.

**Step 2.** Rajesh and Priya operations in PARALLEL — different lock objects. Thread-1 locks rajesh.lock, Thread-2 locks priya.lock — both execute simultaneously.

**Step 3.** Transfer Rajesh→Priya: consistent lock order → lock CUR3001 (Priya, alphabetically first), then lock SAV2001 (Rajesh). Transfer Priya→Rajesh: SAME order → lock CUR3001 first, then SAV2001. No deadlock — both directions acquire locks in the same order.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ PER-ACCOUNT LOCKING ═══

  Global lock (BAD):                Per-account lock (GOOD):
  ALL accounts → 1 lock             Each account → own lock
  [===SEQUENTIAL===]                [Rajesh||Priya||Amit] PARALLEL!
  Throughput: 200 ops/sec           Throughput: 50K ops/sec

  ═══ TRANSFER DEADLOCK PREVENTION ═══

  Thread-1: transfer(Rajesh→Priya)     Thread-2: transfer(Priya→Rajesh)
  Lock order: CUR3001 → SAV2001       Lock order: CUR3001 → SAV2001 (SAME!)
  ├─ lock(CUR3001/Priya) (Recommended) ├─ lock(CUR3001/Priya) → WAIT
  ├─ lock(SAV2001/Rajesh) (Recommended) │  (Thread-1 holds it)
  ├─ debit Rajesh, credit Priya       ├─ Thread-1 finishes → lock(CUR3001) (Recommended) 
  └─ unlock both                       ├─ lock(SAV2001/Rajesh) (Recommended) 
                                       └─ debit Priya, credit Rajesh
  NO DEADLOCK! Consistent ordering!
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Per-Account Lock Design ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Account                    │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  - id: String (final)            │
  │  - lock: Object (private final)  │  ← per-instance lock
  │  - balance: BigDecimal           │  guarded by 'lock'
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + debit(amount): void           │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + credit(amount): void          │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + getBalance(): BigDecimal      │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + getLock(): Object             │  for external multi-account sync
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │      TransferService               │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + transfer(from, to, amt): void  │
  │    1. order = sort by account ID  │  ← deadlock prevention!
  │    2. synchronized(first.lock)    │
  │    3.   synchronized(second.lock) │
  │    4.     from.balance -= amt     │
  │    5.     to.balance += amt       │
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  Pattern: Lock Ordering (prevents deadlock)
  SOLID-S: Account manages its own balance. TransferService manages transfer logic.
  SOLID-D: Transfer depends on Account interface, not implementation.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In a banking app with concurrent account access, use PER-ACCOUNT locks — each Account has its own `private final Object lock`. Operations on different accounts run in PARALLEL (different locks). Operations on the same account are serialized (same lock). Never use a global lock — it makes ALL account operations sequential regardless of which account they access. Use synchronized BLOCKS, not methods — lock only the balance modification, not validation/logging/notification.

For transfers between two accounts: acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (e.g., alphabetically by account ID) to prevent deadlock. Without ordering: Thread-1 locks Rajesh→waits for Priya, Thread-2 locks Priya→waits for Rajesh → DEADLOCK. With ordering: both threads lock CUR3001(Priya) first, then SAV2001(Rajesh) — one waits, gets it after the other finishes → no deadlock. In production banking: combine in-memory per-account locks with database row-level locks (`SELECT FOR UPDATE`) for distributed consistency across multiple JVM instances.

---

keyPoints: synchronized on account object for debit/credit
Prevents race: check balance + debit must be atomic
For transfers: lock both accounts in consistent order
